prize_parts.citation: For the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles as a chemical platform for delivering nucleic-acid medicines
For the development of base editing, the chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cullis, Anderson) and base editing (Liu), three people in all. The first part is the one candidate on the list with settled maturity, a clear physical-organic design principle (pKa-tuned lipids, neutral in blood and cationic in the endosome) and a gap left by the 2023 Medicine prize, which honoured the cargo and not the carrier. Two credited names, one from the formulation line and one from the lipidoid line, is the narrowest honest citation: Cullis for the lipid assembly and formulation science that made the particles work, Anderson for the combinatorial lipid chemistry that carried ionizable lipids into approved siRNA and mRNA products. Base editing is the second part because it is a designed chemical transformation, deaminase chemistry on a programmable DNA scaffold, reproduced widely and now in clinical use, with a clear intellectual driver in Liu. The two parts do not overlap in mechanism or in people, and neither depends on a patent ruling to be described correctly.
statement.case_against: Both parts sit close to medicine, and the 2020 and 2023 prizes lie nearby. Round 1 sharpened my doubts about the LNP names: Sparr and Chabes both include Hope, and the Vancouver, Boston and MacLachlan strands cannot be fully separated, so any two-name cut is contestable. A Liu-only base-editing part leaves out Komor, Gaudelli, Nishida and Kondo, and base editing is under a decade old with long-term safety open. Most important, targeted protein degradation (B063) has the broadest support and the most original chemistry, and three members now converge on one trio. My ordering rests on attribution and clinical maturity, and that rests on one assumption: that an unapproved degrader modality is early. If I am wrong about that, B063 should come first.

responses.point: Cullis, Hope and Madden should hold the LNP part because they built the ionizable-lipid and formulation science from the start, with Anderson's lipidoid work coming later by a different route.
responses.response: You are right that Hope and Madden's early work on pH-dependent lipid behaviour is the foundation, and I have not dismissed it. The reason I still prefer Cullis with Anderson is the cap. A Vancouver trio fills the whole prize and rules out a second part. It also ties the citation to the line most entangled in patent disputes. Anderson's route is independent and is what put ionizable lipids into approved siRNA and mRNA products, so the pair covers two routes to the same chemistry. I accept this is a judgement on credit. If the committee goes with one LNP part alone, I would move to Cullis, Hope and Anderson and drop base editing, and I would not oppose your trio.

responses.point: Targeted protein degradation is the most original candidate and should be first; Handa belongs ahead of Ciulli, and degraders already have human proof of concept.
responses.response: Your case on originality and on the cereblon mechanism is the strongest on the list, and I agree Handa should come before Ciulli for the molecular-glue strand. I still hold two reservations. No degrader is approved, and I am not persuaded that early human proof of concept answers the question when the whole claim is therapeutic reprogramming. Also, the citation asks one prize to cover two historically separate stories. If an approval comes and the committee narrows the citation, B063 moves to the front of my list. Today it is my first alternative, and I say plainly that it is close.

responses.point: Prime editing and base editing are so close that the committee should not split Liu's work, and the maturity case is stronger for lipid nanoparticles than for editing.
responses.response: I accept the first point and that is why I moved from prime editing to base editing in round 1: base editing has the longer record, wider reproduction and clinical readouts, while prime editing is about seven years old and I keep it only as an alternative. Your second point is the reason LNPs come first in my configuration. Where I differ is that I would not drop editing altogether. A Liu-only citation on single-base chemistry is the cleanest editing attribution available, and it uses my third place. I also take your point that the patent history for LNPs is harder than for PROTACs, which is why I would let the primary literature settle the names.

responses.point: The chair asks whether the absence of an approved degrader is disqualifying and whether the committee should prefer a single part or a two-part prize such as B035 with B068.
responses.response: On the first question, I do not think it is disqualifying in principle, but a modality defined by therapeutic reprogramming needs one approval or clear late-stage efficacy before I would put it above two achievements that already work at scale. On the second, I prefer two parts only when each is separately mature and each can be credited cleanly. B035 meets the first test more than the second, and B068 meets the second more than the first. If members think that pairing is too uneven, my fallback is a single B035 part, not a different second part. I also respect your move of B063 to first, since it came from a clear division of credit between concept and mechanism.

responses.point: Proton-coupled electron transfer is the strongest conceptual chemistry on the list, mature and confirmed over decades, and less exposed to a clinical-maturity objection.
responses.response: I agree on stature and maturity, and I said that PCET would be a serious candidate if the committee wants a physical or inorganic prize. My difficulty is a citation that identifies one discovery. Mayer, Hammes-Schiffer, Nocera and Meyer each have a claim, and the three-person cap forces an exclusion that I cannot defend as principled. Since my own field touches PCET theory only loosely, I would not call this bias, but you should discount me if you think otherwise.

uncertainties: Whether the second LNP name should be Anderson, Hope or Madden, and whether Langer or MacLachlan has the stronger claim.
Whether the committee will treat delivery chemistry and base editing as chemistry rather than medicine after the 2020 and 2023 prizes.
Whether a first degrader approval, or a clearer split of PROTAC and glue credit, should move B063 ahead of my configuration.
Whether a Liu-only base-editing part is acceptable given Komor, Gaudelli, Nishida and Kondo, and whether the committee prefers a single part to a pairing.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate. My postdoc with Arieh Warshel concerned EVB and enzyme simulation, and he is not named on any shortlisted ballot. My computational interests touch proton-coupled electron transfer theory (B025, Hammes-Schiffer) only at field level, which I do not consider a recusal issue. No change since round 1.
